title: Conditional performance and transferability of ecological technologies for sustainable water systems: evidence from three decades of EU Framework Programmes
content: Ecological technologies, often coupled with engineered support, are increasingly used for water treatment, hydrological regulation, water reuse, and resource recovery, yet their performance varies across configurations and environmental settings and is difficult to compare and transfer across projects. We critically synthesized evidence from 46 EU Framework Programme projects spanning FP5 to Horizon Europe, drawing on 390 unique academic outputs, 336 project documents, and 25 official project websites. The portfolio was characterized by water type, ecological technology, implementation scale, and environmental setting, and performance evidence was compared across three functional domains: pollutant treatment and water-quality regulation; hydrological retention, storage, and recharge; and resource recovery and productive reuse. The portfolio covered diverse water types and scales but remained concentrated in treatment wetlands, decentralized applications, and European cases. Across all three domains, performance was conditional on influent or rainfall characteristics, hydraulic and climatic conditions, site properties, biological components, system configuration, and operation. Engineered support and process hybridization, including aeration, reactive or conductive media, flow control, advanced treatment, and monitoring, could extend operating envelopes or stabilize target functions, but also introduced energy, material, maintenance, and control requirements. Cross-project comparison was constrained by differences in performance definitions, sampling and calculation methods, monitoring duration, comparators, system boundaries, and evidence provenance. The reviewed evidence therefore supports recurring condition–process–performance relationships, but not pooled performance values, universal thresholds, or context-independent technology rankings. For water process engineering, transferability depends on explicit operating envelopes that allow reproducibility, scalability, and applicability to be assessed across contexts.
